clinicalPearls: A distinct subtype of renal cell carcinoma thought to arise from the intercalated cells of the collecting duct
Generally carries a more favourable prognosis than clear cell carcinoma of comparable stage
Often detected incidentally as a well-circumscribed solid renal mass on imaging
Histology shows large pale cells with prominent cell membranes and perinuclear haloes; the classic and eosinophilic variants are recognised
Multiple chromophobe tumours or oncocytic lesions should raise suspicion of Birt-Hogg-Dube syndrome
Sarcomatoid change, when present, denotes a markedly worse outlook
Distinguishing it from benign oncocytoma can be difficult on imaging and sometimes on biopsy
reference.pathophysiology: Chromophobe renal cell carcinoma is believed to originate from the intercalated cells of the cortical collecting duct. It is characterised molecularly by widespread chromosomal losses affecting several chromosomes, producing a hypodiploid genome. The tumour cells accumulate abnormal microvesicles in the cytoplasm, giving the characteristic pale, flocculent appearance. Compared with clear cell carcinoma, it tends to be more indolent, although sarcomatoid dedifferentiation can transform it into an aggressive tumour.
additionalDifferentials: Eosinophilic solid and cystic renal tumour
additionalInvestigations: Contrast-enhanced CT or MRI to characterise the renal mass and stage disease
Renal mass biopsy where diagnosis will change management
Immunohistochemistry (including CK7 and other markers) to separate it from oncocytoma
Family and personal history assessment for Birt-Hogg-Dube features
Baseline renal function and staging investigations for larger or symptomatic tumours
redFlags: Rapid growth or new symptoms in a previously stable renal mass
Radiological features suggesting locally advanced or metastatic disease
Cutaneous fibrofolliculomas or lung cysts suggesting a hereditary syndrome
reference.prognosis: Localised chromophobe carcinoma generally has an excellent prognosis after surgical excision; outlook worsens substantially with higher stage, tumour necrosis or sarcomatoid transformation.
pitfalls: Confusing it with benign oncocytoma and either over- or under-treating
Missing an underlying Birt-Hogg-Dube syndrome when tumours are multiple
Assuming an indolent course when sarcomatoid change is present
Relying on imaging alone to exclude malignancy in an oncocytic-appearing mass
references: WHO Classification of Urinary and Male Genital Tumours
management: Localised disease is managed with the same stage/size-based surgical framework as RCC generally, individualised to tumour size, complexity, renal function, and comorbidity, by a urologist experienced in RCC
Partial (nephron-sparing) nephrectomy is favoured for small to medium tumours when feasible to preserve renal function
Radical nephrectomy is used for larger, complex, or locally advanced tumours; routine ipsilateral adrenalectomy is no longer performed unless there is direct invasion or a suspicious adrenal lesion

Thermal ablation is a kidney-sparing option for small masses, particularly with high operative risk, but carries a higher local-failure rate and can complicate histological confirmation and follow-up imaging
Active surveillance with imaging follow-up suits small, indolent-appearing masses, especially in older or comorbid patients

No trial evidence specific to chromophobe histology supports adjuvant systemic therapy after resection; the one positive adjuvant trial for a VEGF-pathway tyrosine kinase inhibitor enrolled clear-cell-predominant disease only and does not generalise, so routine adjuvant therapy is not established practice outside a trial

Advanced or metastatic disease is grouped with non-clear-cell RCC for systemic treatment, is generally less responsive to therapy than clear-cell disease, and warrants early referral to medical oncology with strong consideration of clinical trial enrolment
An mTOR inhibitor (everolimus) appears to have relatively stronger activity in chromophobe tumours than in other non-clear-cell subtypes

General RCC practice favours immune-checkpoint-inhibitor-based combination therapy (such as a VEGF-pathway tyrosine kinase inhibitor plus an anti-PD1 agent) as initial treatment for advanced disease, with single-agent tyrosine kinase inhibitor therapy in the refractory setting and the mTOR inhibitor pushed to third line and beyond, though combining it with a tyrosine kinase inhibitor may allow earlier use in the second line

This systemic therapy evidence is extrapolated from broader RCC trials rather than chromophobe-specific studies, so treatment selection should follow standard non-clear-cell RCC guideline pathways (NCCN-consistent) with a strong bias toward offering a clinical trial
Sarcomatoid dedifferentiation denotes markedly worse behaviour and should prompt more aggressive systemic treatment intent and closer monitoring

Multiple or bilateral chromophobe or oncocytic tumours, early age of onset, or a suggestive family or personal history should prompt referral for genetic counselling and germline testing for Birt-Hogg-Dube syndrome, with screening for pulmonary cysts and skin lesions in confirmed cases

Follow-up after treatment of localised disease should be risk-stratified with surveillance imaging extending to around five years, since a meaningful proportion of recurrences occur later; baseline and follow-up renal function should be checked, especially after nephron-sparing surgery or in patients with a single kidney

Refer to urology at diagnosis for surgical planning, to medical oncology for locally advanced or metastatic disease, to clinical genetics when Birt-Hogg-Dube syndrome is suspected, and to a uro-oncology multidisciplinary team for sarcomatoid features or diagnostic uncertainty
